extracted.intended_audience: researchers, clinicians, and students using the Humor Styles Questionnaire (personality/clinical psychology) and test administrators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for using, scoring, and interpreting the Humor Styles Questionnaire (HSQ), a 32‑item self‑report psychometric scale that measures four humor styles for research and clinical work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affiliative Humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterized by the use of humor to amuse others, facilitate relationships, and reduce interpersonal tension. This is generally considered a positive, other-focused style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affiliative subscale items (32-item version): items 1, 5, 9, 13, 17, 21, 29. Note: some items may be reverse-scored. Affiliative humor typically correlates positively with self-esteem, positive affect, and life satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-enhancing Humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Involves maintaining a humorous outlook on life, even during adversity, and using humor as a healthy coping mechanism to regulate emotion. This is a positive, self-focused style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-enhancing subscale items (32-item version): items 2, 6, 10, 14, 18, 22, 30. Self-enhancing scores typically correlate positively with self-esteem, positive affect, and life satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggressive Humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Defined by the use of sarcasm, teasing, ridicule, or disparagement aimed at others. This style often disregards the feelings of others and is considered negative and other-focused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggressive subscale items (32-item version): items 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23, 31. Aggressive humor often correlates with indicators of hostility and related negative outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-defeating Humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Involves excessive self-disparagement, allowing others to laugh at one’s expense, and using humor to hide negative emotions or seek acceptance. This style is considered negative and self-focused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-defeating subscale items (32-item version): items 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 32. Self-defeating humor often correlates with anxiety, depression, and other negative mental-health indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument format and administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Test Type: Self-report questionnaire / Psychometric Scale. Format: 32 items rated on a 7-point Likert scale (1 = Totally Disagree, 7 = Totally Agree).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically administered to adolescents and adults (usually 16 years and older). Respondents rate agreement with each statement; scoring involves summing or averaging item responses for each of the four subscales. Widely translated into multiple languages (e.g., German, Spanish, Chinese, Turkish). Commonly used in college, clinical, and community samples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring method (32-item)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scoring involves summing or averaging item responses for each of the four subscales (Affiliative, Self-enhancing, Aggressive, Self-defeating).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the provided scoring keys mapping items to subscales (Affiliative: 1,5,9,13,17,21,29; Self-enhancing: 2,6,10,14,18,22,30; Aggressive: 3,7,11,15,19,23,31; Self-defeating: 4,8,12,16,20,24,32). Apply reverse scoring where indicated by the original instrument. Scores per subscale represent habitual use of that humor style.

rubrics_metrics.name: 16-item short version scoring and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: A shortened 16-item version exists with alternate subscale formulas and interpretation thresholds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring rules given on page: Put-down humor = start with numeral 14 + answers for questions 1 and 9 − responses to questions 5 and 15; Bonding humor = start with numeral 7 + answers for questions 3 and 10 − responses to questions 6 and 14; Hate-me humor = add answers to questions 2, 12, 13 and 16; Laughing at life = start with numeral 3 + answers for questions 4, 7 and 8 − response to question 11. Interpretation (16-item): scores above 17 = high, 11–17 = average, 11 or under = low.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct validity
rubrics_metrics.description: The HSQ measures the construct of Humor Styles conceptualized along positive vs. negative effects and self-focused vs. other-focused targets, producing four primary constructs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct validity is supported by the consistent four-factor structure observed across diverse samples and alignment with the theoretical model; the scale differentiates adaptive versus maladaptive humor uses for research on well-being and social interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion validity (differential correlations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criterion validity is evidenced by differential correlations of the four humor styles with personality traits and mental-health indicators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affiliative and Self-enhancing humor typically correlate positively with self-esteem, positive affect, and life satisfaction; Aggressive and Self-defeating humor correlate positively with hostility, anxiety, and depression. Use these known patterns when interpreting subscale scores in applied research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability (internal consistency and test–retest)
rubrics_metrics.description: The HSQ demonstrates strong internal consistency and temporal stability across its four subscales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported Cronbach’s alpha (internal consistency): Affiliative 0.80; Self-enhancing 0.81; Aggressive 0.77; Self-defeating 0.80. Test–retest (temporal stability): Affiliative 0.85; Self-enhancing 0.81; Aggressive 0.80; Self-defeating 0.82. These coefficients indicate reliable, stable measurement over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor analysis confirmation
rubrics_metrics.description: Factor analysis supported the hypothesized four-factor solution, showing the 32 items cluster into four distinct yet related dimensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original factor analyses indicated the four factors account for a significant portion of variance in humor usage; this robust structure underpins cross-cultural and research applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissions, commercial use, and provenance
rubrics_metrics.description: The HSQ is commonly used for non-commercial academic research without fees, but permission should be sought from primary author(s) for extensive use or modification. The instrument was developed and published in 2003.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek author permission for commercial uses, translations, or modifications. The instrument text has appeared in various publications (e.g., Psychology Today, 2006) and is available via sources such as ResearchGate (reference provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Item preservation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: IMPORTANT: The following scale items must be preserved in their original language and must not be changed in any way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not alter item wording when administering or adapting the instrument; preserving original items is required to maintain validity and comparability across studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population and sampling considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Intended/population use: general population (primarily adolescents and adults), widely used in college student samples, clinical populations, and diverse community samples globally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical minimum age ~16 years. When applying across cultures or languages, consider validated translations and re-examine factor structure and reliability in the new sample.
